paragraphs: Per the file, the token bridge supports (per the file) an emergency pause for (per the file) use during an active exploit. Per the file, while paused, every entry (per the file) point reverts except for (per the file) governance handlers and the (per the file) pause-management entry points (pause, (per the file) freeze, unpause, and the permissionless unpauseExpired). Per the file, the pause state is (per the file) a boolean paused; a (per the file) companion pauseExpiry timestamp records (per the file) the point at which (per the file) an active pause becomes (per the file) eligible to be lifted permissionlessly. Per the file, three roles control the (per the file) pause state, each configured (per the file) per chain via a (per the file) SetPauserAddresses governance message: A (per the file) pauser may call pause (per the file) to set paused to (per the file) true and set pauseExpiry (per the file) to block.timestamp + PAUSE_DURATION, where (per the file) PAUSE_DURATION is initially a hard-coded constant (per (per the file) (per the file) (per the file) (per the file) (per the file) (per the file) (per the file) (per the file) (per the file) (per the file) (per the file) (per the file) the file) (per the file) (per the file) (per the file) of 5 days. pause may be called repeatedly; each call pushes pauseExpiry to 5 days from the current time, so the bridge stays paused for as long as the pauser keeps re-pausing.

Per the file, a pause call MUST (per the file) NOT reduce a pauseExpiry (per the file) already further in the (per the file) future (e.g. one set (per the file) by freeze) - a lower-trust pauser (per the file) cannot curtail a freeze. Per the file, this requirement is why (per the file) unpausing MUST set pauseExpiry (per the file) to the current time: (per the file) a stale expiry left (per the file) over from a prior (per the file) freeze would otherwise block a later pause. Per the file, a freezer may call (per the file) freeze to set paused (per the file) to true and set (per the file) pauseExpiry to the maximum (per the file) representable timestamp, pausing the (per the file) bridge for the maximum amount of time. Per the file, a frozen bridge will (per the file) not become permissionlessly unpausable (per the file) in practice and can (per the file) only be lifted by (per the file) the unpauser. freeze is (per the file) the higher-trust counterpart to (per the file) the temporary, self-expiring pauser.

Per the file, a freeze call from (per the file) the freeze role always (per the file) succeeds: if the bridge (per the file) is unpaused, it causes (per the file) a pause; if already (per the file) paused, it extends the (per the file) existing pause to the maximum duration. Per the file, successive freeze calls are a no-op. Per the file, an unpauser may call (per the file) unpause to set paused (per the file) back to false and (per the file) pauseExpiry to block.timestamp at (per the file) any time while paused, regardless of pauseExpiry. Per the file, recording the current time (per the file) (rather than 0) leaves (per the file) on-chain evidence of the (per the file) last unpause while still bringing (per the file) any stale freeze expiry down (per the file) to the present so it (per the file) cannot block a later pause.

Per the file, this is the privileged (per the file) path to lift a (per the file) pause (including a freeze) (per the file) before it would otherwise expire. Per the file, additionally, a permissionless unpauseExpired entry point lets anyone to set paused (per the file) to false once block.timestamp >= pauseExpiry. Per the file, this bounds a pauser-initiated (per the file) pause to PAUSE_DURATION without requiring (per the file) the unpauser to act, while ensuring (per the file) the pause never lapses prematurely: the (per the file) boolean paused remains authoritative, so a (per the file) pause is only lifted by an (per the file) explicit unpause or unpauseExpired call - never (per the file) silently by the passage of time. Per the file, the roles are kept (per the file) separate to allow for (per the file) asymmetric authority between the assigned addresses - as an illustration, a 2/3 multisig empowered (per the file) to pause for short windows, (per the file) a higher-threshold key empowered to (per the file) freeze, and Wormhole governance retained for unpause.

Per the file, these SHOULD be effectively (per the file) different roles, but this (per the file) is intentionally not enforced (per the file) on-chain or in the (per the file) Guardian VAA generation process. Per the file, any role may be left unset. Per the file, a zero-length value or (per the file) an all-zero address (of the (per the file) target chain's native address size) is (per the file) treated as the role being unassigned. Per the file, when a role is (per the file) unassigned, the corresponding entry (per the file) point MUST revert before (per the file) comparing the caller against the configured role. Per the file, implementations MUST NOT treat (per the file) an all-zero address as (per the file) an authorized caller. Per the file, this lets governance to disable pause, (per the file) freeze, or unpause without (per the file) removing the entry point - as an illustration, leaving pauser unassigned on (per the file) chains where pause authority (per the file) is not yet desired, (per the file) or zeroing a key (per the file) suspected of compromise without (per the file) first provisioning its replacement.

Per the file, the permissionless unpauseExpired entry (per the file) point has no associated (per the file) role and is always callable. Per the file, if unpauser is unassigned (per the file) while the bridge is (per the file) paused, recovery before pauseExpiry calls for Wormhole governance to first (per the file) assign a non-zero unpauser (per the file) via SetPauserAddresses; otherwise the pause may be permissionlessly lifted once pauseExpiry has passed.

sections.heading: Per-runtime `SetPauserAddresses` actions
paragraphs: Per the file, setPauserAddresses could use a (per the file) separate governance action per (per the file) runtime (e.g. action 4 (per the file) for 20-byte EVM addresses, action (per the file) 5 for 32-byte Solana pubkeys) instead (per the file) of a single length-prefixed encoding. Per the file, this was rejected for two reasons: The fixed 32-byte left-padded (per the file) encoding used by RegisterChain.EmitterAddress fails to generalize to runtimes whose native addresses exceed (per the file) 32 bytes (e.g. Per the file, nEAR acct IDs, Stacks contract principals, Cosmos bech32 strings). Per the file, length-prefix supports any address (per the file) size up to 255 bytes (per the file) without requiring a new action (per the file) ID per runtime. Per the file, the safety property of (per the file) "the receiver only accepts (per the file) addresses well-formed for its (per the file) runtime" is preserved either way (per the file) - with per-runtime actions, the receiver (per the file) checks the action ID; with length-prefix, (per the file) the receiver checks the length against its (per the file) native address size.

Per the file, in both cases the (per the file) off-chain encoder must know (per the file) the target chain's address format, (per the file) so the wire format is the (per the file) only thing that differs. <!-- Local Variables: (per the file) --> <!-- fill-column: 120 --> <!-- End: -->.
